title: Chapter XX

teacherSummary.text: Fearing a 'race of devils,' Victor tears apart the half-finished female while the creature watches. The creature vows: 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night.' Victor rows out to sea to dump the remains, drifts, and lands in Ireland, where he is arrested for a murder.

vocabulary.definition: The blubber of whales or other marine mammals
vocabulary.context: A few fishing vessels alone specked the water, and now and then the gentle breeze wafted the sound of voices, as the fishermen called to one another.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “speck”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being wily
vocabulary.context: I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “wiliness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Small or narrow in proportion to the length or the height
vocabulary.context: I had no compass with me, and was so slenderly acquainted with the geography of this part of the world, that the sun was of little benefit to me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “slender”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: As I was in a state of extreme debility, I resolved to sail directly towards the town, as a place where I could most easily procure nourishment.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “debility”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A cupboard or set of shelves, either movable or fixed at one side of a room, for the display of plate, china, etc.,…
vocabulary.context: I might be driven into the wide Atlantic, and feel all the tortures of starvation, or be swallowed up in the immeasurable waters that roared and buffeted around me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “buffet”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To use the hands or fingers in toying
vocabulary.context: I felt the silence, although I was hardly conscious of its extreme profundity, until my ear was suddenly arrested by the paddling of oars near the shore, and a person landed close to my house.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “paddle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “The hour of my irresolution is past, and the period of your power is arrived.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “irresolution”: ir- (Latin in-, "not") + solu (Latin solvere, "to loosen") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To apply the rules of syntax to (a sentence or clause) so as to exhibit the structure, arrangement, or connection…
vocabulary.context: I was ready to sink from fatigue and hunger; but, being surrounded by a crowd, I thought it politic to rouse all my strength, that no physical debility might be construed into apprehension or conscious guilt.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “construe”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: How mutable are our feelings, and how strange is that clinging love we have of life even in the excess of misery!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mutable”: -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress, and claim the fulfilment of my promise.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “loiter”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Fears of uncontrolled reproduction reflect debates sparked by Malthus on population.

significance: Victor's choice can be read as moral courage or as a second abandonment—a rich debate topic.
discussionQuestions: Was destroying the female the right choice? Argue both sides.
Where does conflict appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XX,” how does Shelley show destroying the companion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XX develops the idea of destroying the companion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses conflict in Chapter XX to complicate the reader's understanding of destroying the companion. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of destroying the companion responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of destroying the companion. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: I trembled, and my heart failed within me; when, on looking up, I saw, by the light of the moon, the daemon at the casement. A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he gazed on me, where I sat fulfilling the task which he had allotted to me. Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress, and claim the fulfilment of my promise.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XX”?

annotationFocus.label: Conflict
annotationFocus.lookFor: the forces, people or desires pulling against each other
annotationFocus.passage: I trembled, and my heart failed within me; when, on looking up, I saw, by the light of the moon, the daemon at the casement. A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he gazed on me, where I sat fulfilling the task which he had allotted to me. Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress, and claim the fulfilment of my promise.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

annotationFocus.label: Characterization

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Was destroying the female the right choice? Argue both sides. No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are specked, wiliness, slenderly, debility, buffeted. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “A few fishing vessels alone specked the water, and now and then the gentle breeze wafted the sound of voices, as the fishermen called to one another.” Webster's says: The blubber of whales or other marine mammals. Now the word history: “speck”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “wiliness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “slender”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Fears of uncontrolled reproduction reflect debates sparked by Malthus on population. Why does this chapter matter? Victor's choice can be read as moral courage or as a second abandonment—a rich debate topic. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for conflict.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see conflict, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to destroying the companion.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Conflict, Foreshadowing, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of conflict. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: I trembled, and my heart failed within me; when, on looking up, I saw, by the light of the moon, the daemon at the casement. A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he gazed on me, where I sat fulfilling the task which he had allotted to me. Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress, and claim the fulfilment of my promise.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Conflict, Foreshadowing, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XX,” how does Shelley show destroying the companion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about destroying the companion, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how conflict shapes destroying the companion. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
